questions.stem: A student sets up three groups of cress seeds: Group A has water, warmth, and oxygen; Group B has water and warmth but is sealed in a container with no oxygen; Group C has water and oxygen but is kept in a fridge at 4 degrees C. Which group is most likely to germinate successfully?

options.text: Group B, because seeds do not need oxygen to germinate
Group C, because cold temperatures promote germination
Group A, because germination requires water, warmth, and oxygen
All three groups will germinate equally well

questions.explanation: Germination requires three conditions: water (to activate enzymes and swell the seed), warmth (to provide the right temperature for enzyme activity), and oxygen (for aerobic respiration to release energy for growth). Group A has all three. Group B lacks oxygen. Group C lacks sufficient warmth. Note that light is NOT required for germination.

questions.stem: During early germination, the seedling relies on food reserves stored in the cotyledons (seed leaves). These reserves are mainly starch. Why does the seed convert starch to glucose during germination?

options.text: Glucose is needed for photosynthesis in the new leaves
Glucose is soluble and can be transported to growing cells, and is used in respiration to release energy for growth
Starch is toxic to the growing embryo and must be broken down
Glucose makes the seed taste sweet to attract animals for dispersal

questions.explanation: Starch is an insoluble storage molecule. During germination, enzymes (amylase) break starch down into soluble glucose, which can be transported to growing points of the seedling. Glucose is then used in aerobic respiration to release energy for cell division and growth, and as a building block for making cellulose for new cell walls.

questions.stem: A gardener soaks bean seeds in water for 24 hours before planting. Why might this help germination?

options.text: Soaking removes toxins from the seed coat
Water softens the seed coat and activates enzymes inside the seed, speeding up the start of germination
The water provides minerals that the seed needs to grow
Soaking heats the seeds to the right temperature for germination

questions.explanation: Water absorption (imbibition) is the first step of germination. Soaking the seeds allows them to absorb water quickly, which softens the seed coat (testa), swells the seed, and activates enzymes that begin breaking down food reserves. This gives the seed a head start, so germination begins more quickly once planted.

questions.stem: An experiment compares germination rates at 10 degrees C, 20 degrees C, 30 degrees C, and 50 degrees C. The highest germination rate is at 30 degrees C, and no seeds germinate at 50 degrees C. What explains the result at 50 degrees C?

options.text: The seeds absorbed too much water at high temperature
The high temperature denatured the enzymes needed for germination, preventing metabolic reactions
Seeds need cold temperatures to break dormancy
At 50 degrees C, oxygen is not available for the seeds

questions.explanation: Germination depends on enzyme activity (e.g., amylase to break down starch). At 50 degrees C, the enzymes denature - their active sites permanently change shape, so they can no longer catalyse the reactions needed for germination. At 30 degrees C, enzyme activity is at its optimum, producing the highest germination rate.

questions.stem: During germination, the radicle (embryonic root) always grows downward, while the plumule (embryonic shoot) grows upward. What controls this directional growth?

options.text: The radicle grows towards water in the soil, and the plumule grows towards the warmest direction
Gravity causes the radicle to grow downward (positive gravitropism) and the shoot to grow upward (negative gravitropism), controlled by the plant hormone auxin
The seed coat directs the radicle downward and the plumule upward
The radicle is heavier than the plumule, so gravity pulls it down

questions.explanation: The directional growth of roots and shoots is controlled by gravitropism (response to gravity). The plant hormone auxin accumulates on the lower side of a horizontal root or shoot. In roots, high auxin concentration inhibits growth, causing the root to bend downward (positive gravitropism). In shoots, high auxin stimulates growth, causing the shoot to bend upward (negative gravitropism).
